name: Green Grey
lede: Green grey is a descriptive name for a muted green with a good deal of grey in it; it is not a pigment or a dye, and the books use the phrase for many different things.

sections.title: A description, not a material
sections.body:
No book in our collection treats green grey as a color with its own history. It turns up as a pair of words in lists, and each author means a different shade [1][2]. The honest summary is that the name points to a region of the color space, where green is dulled by grey, and that real examples come from painting, uniforms, stones and rooms.

On screen, this swatch is close to [[grey-green]] and [[sage-green]], and the two orderings of the words are used for almost the same color [7]. In the same way [[khaki]] sits nearby, and [[olive-green]] is its more yellow cousin [7].

sections.title: Where books put it
sections.body:
Pastoureau notes that artists in the modern period reduced the sea to three dominant colors: green, grey and blue. He points to the young Monet's Green Wave, painted in 1866-67 with a dark, saturated green, as a violent image of the sea unlike what his Impressionist friends later offered [2]. The khaki of military uniforms falls somewhere between green, grey, yellow and brown [3]. Pastoureau separately discusses the greenish grey of German uniforms, feldgrau, which he says recalled an everyday office green [3].

The dictionary lists green, grey or yellow-brown as the possible colors of an imprimatura, the thin primer laid on a gessoed canvas [4]. A diamond cutter quoted by Finlay lists the awkward stones he came to love as gray-green, brown, bottle-green, gray-yellow and yellow-khaki, so the pair of words also turns up in the trade's talk about stone color [5].

Birren in 1950 recommended soft variations of green, grey and blue where critical seeing tasks are done, and cool tones for chronic hospital patients facing a long stay [6]. This is old opinion rather than modern evidence.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
The swatch measures a lightness of 58 and a chroma of about 23, with a hue angle near 137 degrees, which is a green well below the vividness of a hue name [7]. Its contrast ratio against white is 3.4 to 1 [7]. The nearest named colors are Grey Green and American Green at about 5 units, then Sage Green at about 5.5 [7].

We have no archive count for this swatch, so we make no claim about how often it appears in paintings. Screen colors are approximate [7].
